<description>
Modifies the script interpreter to represent stack elements internally using smart pointers, making duplication memory-cheap, and giving us caching keys which are cheap and guaranteed unique by the compiler. First part of a 2-part project to improve script interpreter performance in preparation for PQ signatures.

No consensus changes - a pure performance improvement refactor.

## Motivation

We presently have `MAX_SCRIPT_ELEMENT_SIZE = 520`, but in the near future, motivated by the need for PQ signature schemes, we may want to introduce soft fork changes which increase the max stack element size for new output types well into the multi-kilobyte range. This may be perhaps as high as 10kb or more given the current landscape of PQ signature schemes' sizes.

Ongoing related work:

- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/main/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size
- https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/pull/76

This poses a new problem to today's implementations if deployed naively.

Today's Bitcoin script interpreter moves around raw mutable byte vectors to represent stack elements. When those elements are duplicated, the underlying byte vectors are deep-copied. When hash opcodes execute, they always invoke the corresponding hash function and fully ingest the top stack element. Duplication and hashing cost only a single weight unit in tapscript, with no upper limit on how many times they can be executed, aside from implicit limits due to the 10,000 byte script size maximum.

If we were to simply up the stack element size limit from 520b to 10kb, then we exacerbate an existing DoS vector on bitcoin nodes: Push a big (today 520b, maybe someday 10kb) stack element, then duplicate and hash it over and over. Worst case would be a script like this:

```cpp
<big_blob> DUP DUP [DUP3 RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP RMD160 DROP]...
```

...with the `[...]` part repeating up to the script size limit. RMD160 is used because it lacks hardware acceleration support and so performs significantly worse than even HASH256 or HASH160, making a more effective CPU attack.

This costs the attacker only \~20000 weight units (10kb for the script, 10kb for the stack element), but forces all validators to evaluate OP_RIPEMD160 about 4284 times, each on the same 10kb input. That's about 672588 RMD160 compressions in software.

I ran a benchmark (not in this PR) using this style of script with 520b and 10kb script elements.

- 520b: validation takes about **3 milliseconds**
- 10,000b: validation takes about **52 milliseconds**

## This PR

(idea credit: EthanHeilman)

To address this risk, we would want to implement a **hash cache** for all the hashing opcodes. However, to implement such a cache safely in consensus, we need extremely robust cache keys. A collision in the cache key would be a consensus bug because the cache would return the wrong hash for a given input. But we can't cryptographically hash the inputs to compute a cache key... that is the same work we are trying to avoid with the cache.

Instead we can kill two birds with two PRs.

1. Replace stack elements with ref-counting pointers, so OP_DUP et al duplicate pointers and not the underlying raw bytes. :arrow_backward:  **THIS PR**
2. Implement a hash cache keyed by the stack element pointers. Each cache entry holds a handle to the key pointer so that the key doesn't get dropped and the pointer reallocated for a new stack element (which would cause a consensus bug). Cache key uniqueness is guaranteed by the compiler.  :arrow_backward: **Future PR**

Stage 1 reduces the asymmetric memory inflation attack allowed by OP_DUP et al. Stage 2 fixes the asymmetric CPU DoS attack. To be clear, neither stage fully prevents an attacker from uploading a series of large stack elements, and duplicating/hashing them. But we **do** force attackers to pay for those operations with fees and block space.

I have both stage 1 and 2 implemented locally and can show benchmarks to prove the effect of the cache, if desired. I could have submitted it all as one PR but both stages are atomic and could do well with separate review.
</description>

I started reading the proposal, and the branching inside `OP_CHECKSIG` on whether the signature is stateful or stateless feels a bit icky; those are two different schemes, and bundling them into one leaf checksig is where some of the complexity comes from?

I think it'd be better to split them into separate BIPs for stateful SHRINCS and stateless SHRINCS, and commit both as leaves in a taproot tree. Then which scheme runs is decided by the leaf you reveal, not by checking the signature mid-opcode eval. (I'd recommend this even if we end up increasing the script element size.)

On the variable-size point from [full explanation here](https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/4fe68e3a68fd58be6b0e19436ff6fb7a3357a291/leaf-version-0xC2.mediawiki#user-content-Relaxing_the_Max_Stack_Element_Size), splitting actually makes it okayish. The stateless leaf is fixed-size, a fixed n-element read, no decisions. The stateful leaf is variable, and we can do like a self-delimiting read, read chunks into the verifier, which already has the length from an indicator byte in the first chunk, and stop once it has that many bytes capped at a max.
This way, no spender supplied count, the stop comes from the signature's own (verified) length, so a lie just fails, and the cap means a garbage indicator byte can at worst make you read n elements. Statically then "this opcode pops ≤n, known from the leaf".

(You could instead pad to a fixed n for the stateful leaf with empties to make the pop count constant, but that's a bit of a hack) I think this is a far smaller thing to reason about than multi-KB elements across the whole interpreter (it has a wider scope).

I think this is ideally the same with the current version of the shrincs proposal?,  both leaves under one output are still one address that can always spend, stateful or stateless.

re: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36721#issuecomment-6624074329

Nice benchmarks, thanks for the results.

i should disambiguate here: the multiplexed OP_CHECKSIG defined in that BIP is designed to deploy new signature algorithms like SHRINCS, or maybe someday SQIsign/Falcon/whatever. That BIP doesn't know anything about the stateful vs stateless signing components in SHRINCS. It treats every signature scheme as a black box verification subroutine that takes a triple of byte strings in, and returns success/fail. SHRINCS is defined as one single unified signature scheme within that framework. I should also mention [that BIP is presently being rewritten, to remove SHRINCS-specific language](https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/pull/76)

SHRINCS' verification subroutine does indeed branch based on the signature's leading 'indicator' byte - that is a hard requirement to achieve its design properties. But to the script interpreter, that branching is completely black-box. It is not part of script.

If we chunked signatures into 520b elements though, and relied on the signature itself to tell us how many chunks to pop, we could not use SHRINCS (or any variable-size signature scheme, for that matter) as a black box anymore. Increasing the stack element size limit allows us to keep that black-box compatibility with any signature scheme up to the new size limit.

[Here is the current `shrincs_verify` reference code](https://github.com/SHRINCS/shrincs-bip/blob/4fe68e3a68fd58be6b0e19436ff6fb7a3357a291/SHRINCS.md#shrincs_verify) in case you're interested.

[quoted text omitted]
We did consider a design where the stateful and stateless components are entirely separate schemes, whose keys can be stashed in disjoint tapscript leaves. However this would severely complicate scripting. Think about how you'd design a 2-of-3 multisig output, where each signer has two possible keys they may use, and we don't know which one they'll use until signing time. Every pubkey would need IF/ELSE branching, and every signature would need a true/false decision push (e.g. you sign stateless, i sign stateful, and vice versa, would use completely different pubkeys under this paradigm).
